title: Burned Europe, wildfires as firefly cartography
caption: Left, the whole of Europe from 1 to 27 July 2026. Right, the same treatment applied to the Gironde, where the outline of Bordeaux Métropole gives the scale of the fire.
desc: A month of burnt land across Europe, drawn point by point over satellite imagery.
lede: Every six hectares burnt becomes one glowing point on desaturated satellite imagery. The density of the points carries the extent of the fire, and their halo makes it visible at the scale of a continent.

makingof.intro: Firefly cartography borrows its vocabulary from night imagery: a dark ground, points that radiate. Applied to the burnt land of summer 2026, it makes readable at European scale what a flat red fill would flatten.

steps.d: The technique comes from an article by Jonni Walker for Mapbox, which describes how to obtain this firefly effect by stacking several blurred halos under a bright core. It is applied here to burnt areas rather than to points of interest.

Burnt perimeters are queried from the European EFFIS service, then each polygon is scattered into points, one for every six hectares. Density therefore carries area, which avoids colouring flat shapes. July alone amounts to 65,273 points for 1,662 fires.

Satellite tiles are stitched together then desaturated to keep only the relief. Each point is then composed in four layers: three blurred halos screen-blended, topped by a one-pixel white core. That sharp core over a diffuse halo is what produces the ember effect.

steps.t: Keeping the glow from blowing out
steps.d: At close zoom the points sit only 245 metres apart and their halos overlap enough to turn solid white. The core radius is therefore capped and the halo opacity damped beyond a given magnification.

Labels are placed one after another against an occupancy list, trying twelve positions per fire and eight per city. A fire whose label cannot find room is removed from the map rather than left as a mute ring.

steps.t: A legend true to the map
steps.d: The dot in the legend is drawn with the same four-layer recipe and at the same scale as the map, so the symbol shown to the reader is exactly the one found on the image. The distance bar picks the largest round distance fitting within a fifth of the width, computed at the centre latitude.
On the Gironde frame, the outline of Bordeaux Métropole sits next to the burn scar. Its 28 municipalities and 57,706 hectares give the measure: the fire covers two thirds of the metropolitan area.

makingof.credits: Sources: Copernicus EMS / EFFIS for burnt areas, imagery Esri / Maxar / Earthstar Geographics, Bordeaux Métropole boundary from geo.api.gouv.fr.

title: Europe's wildfires, day by day
caption: The map layers burnt areas, the day's active fires and the smoke carried by the wind. Below, the ten largest fires and the toll by country.
desc: Burnt areas, active fires and smoke across Europe, updated every day.
lede: A map that follows the European fire season and updates itself every morning. It brings together three satellite sources: burnt perimeters, fires detected day by day, and the smoke carried by the wind.

makingof.intro: In July 2026, close to 400,000 hectares burnt across Europe, 157,000 of them in Spain alone. The map answers the question every new episode brings back: where is it burning, and since when? Three satellite datasets answer it, provided they are cleaned, made light enough and refreshed without anyone lifting a finger.

steps.d: Burnt perimeters come from the European EFFIS programme, which maps them by satellite. Active fires come from NASA, through the VIIRS and MODIS detections published in near real time. Smoke comes from the European CAMS forecast, which isolates the share of particles attributed to vegetation fires.

A thermal satellite cannot tell a wildfire from a blast furnace. A filter therefore spots the points that come back to the same place on eight days or more over the period, along with their immediate neighbours, and discards them as permanent industrial sources. Over the month of July, 488 sites were removed from the map that way.
Polygons are simplified and their coordinates rounded, while the smoke grids are compressed by encoding runs of identical values. Readers load a month of hourly data without waiting.

steps.t: A timeline with six steps a day
steps.d: The timeline moves forward in four-hour steps and shows, at each one, the fires detected over the previous twelve hours. Burnt areas, for their part, accumulate from the start of the period, which makes the season visibly build up.

Every morning, a GitHub action reruns the Python scripts, fetches the new data and commits it to the repository. The site is redeployed only when something has changed, which avoids empty publications.
Clicking one of the ten largest fires zooms to its perimeter, with the toll by country alongside. The map embeds into articles via pym.js, in an iframe that adjusts to the height of its content.

makingof.credits: Sources: Copernicus EMS / EFFIS, NASA FIRMS, CAMS (Copernicus / Météo-France). Basemap CARTO Positron / OpenStreetMap.

title: Masculinism, one scroll away on TikTok
caption: The first step of each scroll block. On the left, the bot plays Matteo. On the right, the hour of scrolling is still empty, with its four categories.
desc: A bot plays a 15-year-old on TikTok to measure where the algorithm takes him.
lede: How far can the algorithm take a teenager? To find out without exposing a real minor, we handed the phone to a bot that plays a profile, watches the videos and likes them. We then measure what TikTok serves back.

makingof.intro: Measuring how a TikTok feed drifts means provoking that drift first. The setup combines three parts: a bot that scrolls in a teenager's place, an AI that judges each video and a chart that sums up the hour of scrolling.

steps.t: A bot in a teenager's place
steps.d: We did not want to expose a real minor, so a bot holds the phone. It plays a profile and works through the feed the way a user would, on a real device and with a real account.

steps.t: One persona, one source of truth
steps.d: The profile to play fits in a single configuration sentence, which here describes Matteo, 15, into working out. That sentence alone defines what the bot should find interesting, and changing it is enough to change teenager.
For each item, an AI is given what the screen shows and answers in one line whether the video matches the persona. That verdict decides what happens next.
When a video matches, the bot lingers on it and likes it now and then, sometimes in the first seconds, sometimes at the end. The recommendation feeds on those signals, namely watch time and likes.
Every item encountered is recorded as the session runs. We then sorted the roughly 550 posts from an hour of scrolling into four categories: working out, motivation, masculinist and other.

steps.t: Making the hour of scrolling visible
steps.d: The long read alternates a phone on screen, where videos scroll in step with the text, and a D3 chart where each item seen becomes a bar as thick as the time spent on it. Once grouped, those bars deliver the verdict: in one hour, the bot took in nearly thirteen minutes of masculinist content.

makingof.credits: Investigation: Marie-Laure Mathot and Ambroise Carton. Bot, data extraction and web development: Ambroise Carton.

title: Is it warm or cold for the season?
caption: The daily map places each station against its own normal. The scatter plot sets that same gap in fifty years of measurements.
desc: Belgium's climate in about twenty charts, updated every day.
lede: About twenty charts answer the same question every day: is this normal for the season? They compare temperatures station by station against the 1991-2020 normal and set them in half a century of measurements.

makingof.intro: The dashboard answers a simple question every day: is it warm or cold for the season? It then sets the answer in fifty years of measurements, across about twenty charts fed by the same data chain.

steps.d: Everything starts from the Belgian met office's daily observations, which give the maximum temperature, the minimum temperature and the rainfall of each station. Those values are compared against the 1991-2020 normal, computed day of year by day of year. That departure from the normal is the thread running through every chart.

Every day a Python script calls the met office API again and rewrites the whole available history instead of appending only the latest row. That strategy catches stations that reported late and values corrected after quality control. The script then regenerates the files the app consumes.

Each visualisation lives on its own route and embeds independently into articles via pym.js. The newsroom can therefore drop today's map into one story and the climate stripes into another, with nothing duplicated.

A selector shows the station nearest to you rather than the national average. Each chart also opens on an automatically generated sentence spelling out the day's figure, so the data reads before anyone looks at the curve.

steps.t: From a day to half a century
steps.d: The scales answer each other. The map shows today's departures, the scatter plot tracks daily departures since 1971 with its rolling mean, the climate stripes sum up each year, a module detects records that have fallen and ERA5 global temperature gives the context.
A GitHub action chains the data update and the redeployment to Cloudflare, so the dashboard refreshes with no intervention. The repository documents the calculation choices behind each chart.

title: The 2026 World Cup in a single circle
caption: The round of 32 sits on the outer ring and the champion takes the centre. Clicking a flag opens the match card, statistics included.
desc: The 2026 World Cup knockout bracket unfolded as a circle, from the round of 32 to the final.
lede: A knockout bracket folds into a circle. The 32 teams of the round of 32 sit around the outside, each round tightens inwards and the champion arrives at the centre. Scores update live.
data: Live results from ESPN · video summaries from RTBF

makingof.intro: The project takes an existing idea, a knockout bracket unfolded into a circle, and makes it live. Scores arrive in real time, each match opens a detailed card and the video summaries play without the site ever being rebuilt.

steps.d: The circular bracket, where the knockout tree closes in on the champion, is borrowed from an infographic by Emilio Sansolini. This version offers an interactive rereading of it.

The ESPN API returns a flat list of matches with no hierarchy. A module reconstructs the tree by following the winners and the qualification labels, to recover which match feeds which. A safeguard then checks that each match in a round feeds exactly one match in the next, which stops the bracket from breaking the moment a team qualifies.

The angular order of the sixteen first-round matches comes from a traversal of the tree starting at the final. Each following match sits midway between its two qualifiers and the branches meet through a radial segment then an arc, so no line ever crosses another.

Each team receives a colour taken from its flag, which is kept only if it stays readable in both light and dark themes. Two opponents never share the same hue, the colour of one being shifted if needed. The winner's branch is drawn in their colour and the rest of the bracket stays grey.

At the merge point of each match, the score is written along the axis separating the two flags, so each figure lands opposite its own. Clicking a flag opens the match card, with possession, shots, corners, scorers, cards and recent form. A badge plays RTBF's video summary, fetched daily by a GitHub action.

On load, the flags settle first, then the branches draw themselves round by round in a clockwise sweep. The animation gives way if the system asks for reduced motion. The SvelteKit app is deployed as a static site and embeds into articles via pym.js.

makingof.credits: Original idea: Emilio Sansolini. Live data: ESPN. Video summaries: RTBF Sport.

title: The Tour de France as a bicycle wheel
caption: On the left, the 21 stages form the rim and the hub zooms in on the selected stage, from Gap to Alpe d'Huez. On the right, the battle for the yellow jersey reads stage after stage.
desc: The 21 stages of the 2026 Tour laid out as a bicycle wheel, updated throughout the race.
lede: La Grande Boucle is taken literally. The 21 stages form the rim of a wheel, France fills the hub and the yellow jersey moves along the tyre stage after stage.
data: Official route, GPX tracks and standings (letour.fr)

makingof.intro: The Tour de France is drawn as the thing it is ridden on, a wheel. The 21 stages form the rim, the hub holds the map and the yellow jersey moves along the tyre day after day.

steps.d: An SVG circle is cut into 21 arcs. Each takes a width proportional to the length of its stage and a colour matching its type, whether flat, hilly, mountain or time trial. Two wider gaps mark the rest days and an opening at the top of the wheel separates the Grand Départ from the finish.
A MapLibre map clipped to a circle sits at the centre. It shows France in shaded relief and zooms in on a stage's GPS track as soon as you hover it, with the start and finish towns.

Elevation profiles are redrawn in SVG from the official track. An analyser picks out the hardest climb of the stage and the gradient of the closing kilometres, which makes it possible to describe the route without typing it in by hand.

During the Tour, a scheduled GitHub action reads the official standings from letour.fr several times a day, converts them into compact JSON and redeploys the site. The jerseys, the gaps and the stage winners therefore update on their own.
One tab charts the cumulative gap to the leader for the top eight overall, stage after stage. Another gathers the five official classifications and the route in numbers.
The SvelteKit app is deployed as a static site and embeds into articles via pym.js.

makingof.credits: Sources: official route, GPX tracks and standings from letour.fr · relief Terrain Tiles (Mapzen/AWS) · outlines france-geojson (ODbL) · icons Lucide.

title: Belgium Breakout
caption: Every Belgian municipality is an equal-sized square, coloured by population: a tilegram turned into a brick-breaker.
desc: A brick-breaker where you 'free' Belgian municipalities laid out on a tilegram.
lede: Data is also a game. Belgium Breakout turns the map of Belgium into a brick-breaker. Each municipality becomes a brick, and the more people it has, the deeper blue it gets and the more points it is worth.

makingof.intro: I had wanted to build a tilegram of Belgium for a long time, where every municipality becomes an equal-sized square instead of keeping its real land area. The hard part was placing the municipalities on a Minecraft-like grid while staying geographically faithful.

steps.d: I came across a post by Josep Ferrer explaining exactly how to generate this kind of grid, with his open-source Python library popgrid. The initial roadblock was gone.
From a GeoJSON of Belgian municipalities and a bit of Python, I generate the tilegram: a grid where each municipality occupies one square, placed to stay faithful to the country's geography.
Looking at the result, I thought back to the brick-breaker built by our colleagues at Contexte, and it struck me that the map could be broken.

It is all coded in Svelte. Each municipality becomes a brick coloured by population, so the denser ones turn a deeper blue and are worth more. You aim for the big cities, chain combos and free the country square by square.
I will happily admit that this project is useless. But not everything we make has to be useful, and treating data as a playground is part of the job too.

makingof.credits: Tilegram generated with Josep Ferrer's popgrid library. Game concept inspired by Contexte.

title: Daily tracking of the war in Ukraine in maps
caption: The map of territorial control in Ukraine, on the left. The same tool powered a Middle East version, on the right, built on the same technical foundation and the same ISW data.
desc: Where does the front line stand in Ukraine? An interactive map updated every day.
lede: This map of territorial control in Ukraine updates automatically every day. The daily assessments from the Institute for the Study of War arrive as email attachments, then get unzipped, converted to a geographic format and placed on the map with no manual intervention, which keeps the front line continuously up to date.

makingof.intro: The challenge is to publish a reliable map of the front every day without touching it by hand. The Institute for the Study of War's shapefiles arrive by email in a raw GIS format, and everything else is automated, from the email to the pixel.

steps.d: A Google Apps Script triggered each day queries Gmail, locates the latest ISW email (the most recent by subject date, never an outdated version) and extracts its .zip attachments.
Each archive is unzipped, renamed to a stable layer identifier, then pushed to GitHub via the Git API (blobs + tree + commit). Missing layers are deleted so that obsolete data is never displayed.
A GitHub Actions workflow converts the shapefiles to GeoJSON with shpjs, reprojects from EPSG:3857 to EPSG:4326 and rounds the coordinates to lighten the files.
The SvelteKit app draws the polygons (territorial control, advances, counter-offensives) with MapLibre GL, using a palette and labels designed for editorial reading.

The same workflow rebuilds the site and deploys it to GitHub Pages. The RTBF article embeds it via pym.js in a responsive iframe. No human intervention takes place between the arrival of the email and the publication of the map.

title: RedDeviz: the data of more than 1,000 football matches geolocated
caption: The globe brings together more than 860 matches of the Belgian national teams. The filters isolate competitions, results and notable streaks.
desc: A cartochronology of every match of the Red Devils and the Red Flames.
lede: Every match of the Belgian national teams, placed back in time and space. Hover or click to explore opponents, venues and results across the decades.

makingof.intro: More than a century of matches from the two Belgian national teams come together on a single globe. The visualisation adapts an existing format and applies it this time to the Belgian sides, using official data from the Royal Belgian Football Association.

steps.d: The principle of chronological cartography (a globe where each match is placed in time and space) is directly inspired by the work of Chroniques Bleues on the French national team, spotted via Daniel Breton (Visual Data Flow). RedDeviz is a reinterpretation of it for the Red Devils and the Red Flames.
The matches of the Red Devils and the Red Flames come from the official RBFA data (opponents, dates, venues, results), across the entire history of the national teams.

Each host city is converted into coordinates via Nominatim, the OpenStreetMap geocoding service. A cache avoids re-geocoding the same cities and a disambiguation table corrects ambiguous places, so no coordinate is typed in by hand.

The host country is inferred from the geocoded city, which correctly places matches on neutral ground (Olympics, World Cup, Women's Euro). When the city is missing or unreadable, the marker falls back to the country's capital and is flagged as approximate (never presented as exact).
Node.js scripts consolidate everything into compact JSON files (matches + details), with stadium names in French when they exist, ready to be consumed by the app.
The SvelteKit app projects the matches onto a globe with D3 / d3-geo (TopoJSON basemaps), with filters by competition, result and notable streaks. It embeds into RTBF articles via pym.js.

title: Fuel prices
caption: The ranking of the best prices by province and the fill-up calculator form two embedded widgets that update automatically.
desc: Embeddable widgets on fuel prices in Belgium, refreshed several times a day.
lede: These two widgets grew out of the rise in fuel prices that followed the start of the US and Israeli offensive against Iran. They answer two questions: how much does a tank of fuel cost today compared with a past date, and where can you find the best prices by province? They embed into articles on the RTBF Actus site and refresh automatically via GitHub Actions.

makingof.intro: These two widgets answer, with the figures to back it up, a very concrete question: should you fill up today or wait until tomorrow? They update on their own several times a day and drop straight into an article.

steps.d: The day's rates come from SPF Économie, the history from Statbel (be.STAT, open licence) and the best prices at the pump from carbu.com (with permission), by province and by fuel type.
GitHub Actions workflows scheduled several times a day refresh the data and write compact JSON files, published directly to GitHub Pages without rebuilding the site.
The pipeline handles the pitfalls of public data: for example the change in heating oil nomenclature (H0/H7 since April 2024) is reconciled with the old label to keep a continuous history.

A calculator, which compares the cost of a tank today with that of a past date, and a ranking of the best prices by province share the same Svelte foundation, with a carefully crafted palette and labels.
Each widget embeds into articles on the RTBF Actus site via pym.js (responsive iframe that adapts to the height of the content).

title: 20 km of Brussels: your recap
caption: Type a name or a bib number to place a performance within the distribution of all runners.
desc: Your personal recap of the 20 km of Brussels: where do you stand compared with the other participants?
lede: Tens of thousands of runners share one course and a wealth of finishing times. This multilingual tool places a performance within the full field of participants.
data: Official results of the 20 km of Brussels

makingof.intro: Tens of thousands of runners take the start, and the tool promises each of them a place in the race within seconds. All the work consists of turning a long list of times into a personal, readable narrative.

steps.d: Starting from the official race results, Node.js scripts compute the distributions by category (medians, quantiles, histograms) as well as the intermediate split times (5.5 km, 10 km, 15 km, finish).

steps.t: Finding your place in the crowd
steps.d: These distributions answer the runner's real question: where do I rank? A time or a bib number is compared with the whole field of participants, by sex and by age category.
Para-athletics, classified separately, is handled in its own dataset so it is not lost in the general ranking.
The SvelteKit app turns everything into charts with D3 (scales, interpolations), in an interface available in several languages (in keeping with a Brussels audience).
The site is generated as static and deployed to GitHub Pages, ready to be shared and embedded in RTBF content.

title: 20 km of Brussels: the tough zones
caption: The narrative links the course profile to the observed slowdowns, kilometre by kilometre, according to your runner profile.
desc: The toughest zones of the 20 km of Brussels course, according to your profile.
lede: This scrolling narrative turns the split times of thousands of runners into a reading of the course. It shows the climbs, the fatigue points and the places where the crowd slows down, kilometre by kilometre.
data: Official split times of the 20 km of Brussels

makingof.intro: The reader enters their sex, age and target time, then runs down the course, suffering zone by suffering zone. The editorial question is simple: where does your group really slow down?

steps.d: The starting point gathers thousands of runners' GPS traces shared publicly on Strava. They are grouped into cohorts, five finish-time levels crossed with the two sexes, which makes it possible to reason about comparable groups rather than individuals.

For each cohort, a smoothed pace curve is computed along the course. A suffering zone is detected automatically where the pace markedly exceeds the cohort average (at least 10 s/km over 400 m or more). Each group therefore has its own zones, and the length of the narrative adapts.

Each zone is cross-referenced with the course elevation profile, depending on whether it climbs, stays flat or descends. It comes with a signed pace gap relative to the group's race average and a targeted coaching comment.
The figures displayed respect the reader's age cell when it is well populated, and cleanly fall back to a broader granularity otherwise. A badge always indicates which sample the answer is based on.
All of it is rendered in SvelteKit with D3, which draws the elevation bands, the progress overlays and the pace charts, orchestrated by scrolling for a guided reading.

title: Orthophotos of Wallonia
caption: The lens mode overlays 1971 and 2024: on the left Wallonia, on the right the same comparison over Brussels.
desc: A comparator of aerial imagery of Wallonia and Brussels, from 1971 to today.
lede: How have a neighbourhood, an industrial zone or a forest changed over fifty years? Three modes (lens, before/after and time travel) let you scroll through the orthophotos decade after decade.

makingof.intro: Fifty years of aerial photographs overlay on a single map to show a territory changing. The challenge is to make a mass of official imagery as simple to explore as a slider you drag.

steps.d: The basemaps come from the Walloon Region's geoservices, with one layer per orthophoto vintage from 1971 to 2023, supplemented with historical maps by Ferraris (1770) and Vandermaelen (1850). A variant also covers Brussels, where the imagery goes back to the 1930s.

A lens mode reveals another year under a disc, a before/after mode compares two vintages and an animated timelapse runs through the decades. These three entry points answer the same question: how has this place evolved?
An address search field (geocoder) instantly recentres the map on the place the reader cares about, rather than leaving them to navigate by hand.
The SvelteKit app relies on MapLibre GL to display and synchronise the layers, with a year selector, a welcome tutorial and share buttons.
All of it embeds into articles via pym.js (responsive iframe that adjusts to the height of the content).

steps.t: Two editions, a big audience hit
steps.d: The tool comes in a Wallonia edition and a Brussels edition. Even though this kind of topic has nothing to do with the news cycle, it reached a very large audience and became a genuine traffic hit.

title: Strait of Hormuz: the Iranian stranglehold
caption: The narrative follows the cargo ship Giacometti in near real time thanks to its AIS signal, as it approaches and then reaches the heart of the Persian Gulf.
desc: How Iran tightens, and loosens, its grip on one of the most strategic shipping passages in the world.
lede: By following the cargo ship Giacometti through the strait, this long read shows, AIS signals in hand, how Iranian tensions block nearly 2,000 ships and reshape global traffic.

makingof.intro: This scrollytelling follows a cargo ship, the Giacometti, to tell how Iran opens and closes one of the most strategic shipping passages in the world. The challenge is to make a complex maritime situation readable, step by step.

steps.d: The narrative latches onto the trajectory of a real cargo ship through the strait, reconstructed from its near-real-time position. The ship data comes from Global Fishing Watch.
Beyond a single ship, the article highlights the congestion of the strait and the alternative routes taken when Iran tightens its grip.

The Sentinel-1 radar images see by day as by night and through clouds. They are retrieved and assembled via Python scripts on the Copernicus Data Space, then annotated by hand to point out ship groupings, with circles and labels placed to the pixel.
The story is broken into sections that follow one another as you scroll, from the ship to the "non-hostile ships" and then the blocked vessels, each with its own map and charts in D3.

All of it is built on an in-house article template (title, intro, map, annotated image, callouts, share components), which makes it possible to put together a polished, consistent long read quickly from one topic to the next.

title: Southern Lebanon wiped off the map
caption: Geolocated videos document the destruction village by village. The map, for its part, records the strikes counted across the country.
desc: Israel is razing villages in southern Lebanon with bulldozers and explosives: the proof in images.
lede: Satellite images and geolocated videos document, village by village, the destruction of a buffer zone along the Israeli border.
data: IDF · Reuters · ISW · CNRS · Oregon State University

makingof.intro: The piece documents, with proof in hand, the destruction of villages in southern Lebanon along the Israeli border. The whole challenge is to verify and geolocate what was destroyed, village by village.

steps.d: The opening chains full-screen videos with a MapLibre map shown as an inset, which then expands to fill the screen. Each step of the story has its own camera position, in a desktop and a mobile variant.

Drone videos and images are cross-checked and precisely placed back on the ground, and corroborated with satellite-imagery damage assessments such as those from Oregon State University, to document the destruction in the region.
A MapLibre map overlays the layers of geolocated strikes (more than a thousand dated events) and the buffer zone, to give the scale and geography of the phenomenon.
The article is built on an in-house template that provides the map, the annotated images, the callouts and the grids. It is deployed as a static site, ready to be embedded in RTBF content.

makingof.credits: Sources: IDF, Reuters, ISW, CNRS (Lebanon), Oregon State University.

title: Renee Good, killed by an ICE agent
caption: Surveillance and body-cam videos synchronised on the location, Portland Avenue, to reconstruct the scene second by second.
desc: What the footage of Renee Good's death in Minnesota tells us, second by second.
lede: Body-cam, witness videos and satellite imagery are synchronised and cross-referenced frame by frame in order to reconstruct the scene as precisely as possible and to confront the different accounts.
data: CNN · AFP · Reuters · DHS · metadata analysis

makingof.intro: The story reconstructs, second by second, the death of Renee Good, killed by an ICE agent in Minnesota. The goal is to confront the visual sources in order to offer the most precise possible reconstruction of the scene, without ruling in place of the investigation.

steps.d: The work relies on open source intelligence techniques. Surveillance, body-cam and witness videos are collected and verified, then cross-referenced with satellite imagery of the location.
The different videos are aligned to a single clock from visual cues and timestamp badges, to follow the sequence of events to the second.
The sequence is driven by a spreadsheet describing the steps, the texts, the media and the timestamps. A Python script converts it to JSON, then the videos are optimised for the web.
The scrolling narrative combines a satellite view (MapLibre) of the location and the video sequences, so the reader can place each moment in space as well as in time.

title: The Constellation fire in 3D
caption: On the left, the 3D model of the bar opens the story. On the right, the five witness videos are realigned on the waveform of the track playing that night.
desc: An amateur renovation turned deadly trap: the Constellation fire explained in 3D.
lede: On New Year's night 2026, a bar in Crans-Montana goes up in flames in a matter of seconds. A 3D model of the premises reconstructs the key moments of the evening and the deadly trap the venue became.

makingof.intro: The story explains, room by room, how a ski-resort bar became a death trap in under a minute. The development work consists of putting a 3D model at the service of the text and turning it in step with the reading.

steps.d: The model of the bar comes from Swiss broadcaster RTS, built from photos and videos of the night and from drawings made by survivors during their police interviews. Here it is split into separate parts, the basement, the stairs, the doors and the terraces, so it can be revealed piece by piece.
Nine scrollytelling steps rotate the model and move the camera in Three.js. Each step has its own camera position, its own additional models and its own lighting, in a mobile and a desktop variant.

Framing a 3D scene by hand in code quickly becomes unworkable. An editing page therefore places the camera with the mouse, switches between the two formats and exports the values, which become the single source of truth for the story.

steps.t: OSINT: the music as a clock
steps.d: Five witness videos were gathered, none of them timestamped. The track playing in the bar that night acts as a shared clock: aligning each clip on the waveform of the song recovers their exact position relative to one another and reconstructs the timing of the fire from the moment it started. It was all over within a minute.
A MapLibre map places the bar within the resort and D3 charts give the human toll of the night, drawn from figures published by the Valais cantonal police and the Swiss press.

The story alternates the model with real images. It runs through the timeline of the evening, shows the photos taken before and after the renovation work, brings in witness videos and closes with the two parts of the L'Enquête report.

makingof.credits: Story and analysis: Ambroise Carton with Olivia Grisard. 3D model: RTS. Graphics: Damien Hendrichs (Imagique). Sources: Valais cantonal police, 24heures.ch, RTS.

title: When Musk amplifies the far right
caption: The timeline of posts relayed by Elon Musk brings out the spikes in activity, illustrated by the tweets concerned.
desc: How Elon Musk uses his network X to boost the far right in Europe.
lede: This investigation analyses the posts relayed on X by Elon Musk. It shows what the amplification network around his account reveals and the virality mechanics at work in the rise of the European far right.

makingof.intro: This investigation tells, as scrollytelling, how Elon Musk uses his network X to amplify the far right in Europe. The challenge is to make visible, post by post, virality mechanics that are hard to grasp with the naked eye.

steps.d: The corpus gathers five months of Elon Musk's X posts, starting from the election of Donald Trump. It is then cleaned to allow a chronological, quantified reading.
Each post is classified by topic using artificial intelligence, then the AI's results are systematically verified by the journalists before publication.
The dataset is converted from CSV to the Parquet format (via Apache Arrow), which sharply reduces the weight loaded by the browser and smooths the scrolling, even with large volumes.
The narrative alternates a phone mockup, which shows the real posts, with a data timeline. Each spike in activity becomes readable, animated in D3 with shape morphing via flubber.
The sections follow one another as you scroll, with image preloading and loading-state handling for a seamless reading.
